moveSequence: 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 g6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Bg7 5.e4 Nc6 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7
commentaryText: Now with the benefit of hindsight, I would probably use the 9...Nxd4 move-order, but at the time I stayed loyal to the book!

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen
source.location: Bent Larsen chapter, Bonus Game 2 (Gulko - P.H. Nielsen, Esbjerg 2000)

moveSequence: 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 g6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Bg7 5.e4 Nc6 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Nc2
commentaryText: This is quite a luxurious version of the Nc2 system. White's bishop goes directly to e3, while Black has committed his bishop to d7.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen
source.location: Bent Larsen chapter, Bonus Game 2 (Gulko - P.H. Nielsen, Esbjerg 2000)

moveSequence: 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 g6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Bg7 5.e4 Nc6 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Nc2 a6 11.f3 Rc8 12.Qd2 Re8 13.Rac1 Qa5 14.Na3
commentaryText: Back then, this move was a puzzling move, looking rather passive and without any apparent plan. This is just about as wrong as one can be in judging the opponent's motive as possible, but at least it does bring back the good memories of youthful optimism!

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen
source.location: Bent Larsen chapter, Bonus Game 2 (Gulko - P.H. Nielsen, Esbjerg 2000)

moveSequence: 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 g6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Bg7 5.e4 Nc6 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Nc2 a6 11.f3 Rc8 12.Qd2 Re8 13.Rac1 Qa5 14.Na3 Be6
commentaryText: In hindsight, 14...Ne5 might have looked logical, preventing White's next move, as the c4-pawn would then be hanging. But... then 15.b3!! is possible, as 15...Qxa3 traps the black queen, which means that White can proceed in a similar fashion to the game anyway!

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen
source.location: Bent Larsen chapter, Bonus Game 2 (Gulko - P.H. Nielsen, Esbjerg 2000)

moveSequence: 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 g6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Bg7 5.e4 Nc6 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Nc2 a6 11.f3 Rc8 12.Qd2 Re8 13.Rac1 Qa5 14.Na3 Be6 15.Nab1 Ne5 16.b3 Rb8 17.a3
commentaryText: White has been shuffling his knight backward as well as now weakening his pawn-structure. Yet, my position has turned from what I thought as completely fine to a state of now having absolutely nothing positive to say about it. After the text move, Black cannot play ...b7-b5 which loses a pawn due to 18.cxb5 axb5 19.b4. However, if he cannot play that, he cannot do much other than just sit and wait. The extra set of knights compared to the standard position might at first seem a bit clumsy for White, but as he controls more space, the white extra knights will have more room to manoeuvre, while Black's knights, on the other hand, will start tripping over each other.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen
source.location: Bent Larsen chapter, Bonus Game 2 (Gulko - P.H. Nielsen, Esbjerg 2000)

moveSequence: 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 g6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Bg7 5.e4 Nc6 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Nc2 a6 11.f3 Rc8 12.Qd2 Re8 13.Rac1 Qa5 14.Na3 Be6 15.Nab1 Ne5 16.b3 Rb8 17.a3 Rec8 18.b4
commentaryText: Too soon! Here, 18.f4!? or 18.h3 first, preparing a later f3-f4 by covering the g4-square, would mean Black having to worry about both flanks, leaving him with a very unpleasant position.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen
source.location: Bent Larsen chapter, Bonus Game 2 (Gulko - P.H. Nielsen, Esbjerg 2000)

moveSequence: 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 g6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Bg7 5.e4 Nc6 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Nc2 a6 11.f3 Rc8 12.Qd2 Re8 13.Rac1 Qa5 14.Na3 Be6 15.Nab1 Ne5 16.b3 Rb8 17.a3 Rec8 18.b4 Qd8 19.Nd5 b6
commentaryText: Here 19...b5!? would have created some much need counterplay, as 20.cxb5 axb5 21.Rxc8 Rxc8 22.Bxb5 Nxd5 23.exd5 Bd7 creates almost Benko-like counterplay for the pawn. After the text move, however, he is back to just being passive.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen
source.location: Bent Larsen chapter, Bonus Game 2 (Gulko - P.H. Nielsen, Esbjerg 2000)

moveSequence: 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 g6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Bg7 5.e4 Nc6 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Nc2 a6 11.f3 Rc8 12.Qd2 Re8 13.Rac1 Qa5 14.Na3 Be6 15.Nab1 Ne5 16.b3 Rb8 17.a3 Rec8 18.b4 Qd8 19.Nd5 b6 20.Rfd1 a5 21.h3 axb4 22.axb4 Bd7 23.Na3 Bc6 24.Bf1 Ned7 25.Nc2
commentaryText: As Gulko explained to me after the game: not only did he provide me with half a point, but he also gave a lesson on the pawn structure: "I spend the whole game showing the virtues of keeping four minor pieces on the board, but just like this, I allowed you to swap down to three!" Many other moves would have preserved a white edge, basically anything not allowing Black those liberating exchanges!

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen
source.location: Bent Larsen chapter, Bonus Game 2 (Gulko - P.H. Nielsen, Esbjerg 2000)

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3
commentaryText: White tries to get the same kind of position as in Game 19, but here she has wasted time on 10.Rc1. However, when Black plays the 9...Bd7 move order, there is nothing White can do about this. Black is ready to play ...a7-a5 with the standard dark-square strategy. Instead, White can also play 12.f3, with the exchange of the dark-squared bishops in mind. Here it is important for Black to respond with 12...a5 since 12...Nd7? was severely punished in Razuvaev-Honfi, Cienfuegos 1976. After the thematic 13.b4! Bxd4+ 14.Qxd4 Qb6 15.Qxb6! Nxb6 16.e5! dxe5 17.b5 Be8 18.c5 Nd7 19.Nd5 e6 20.Ne7+ Kg7 21.c6 Black was unable to stop the c-pawn. But if Black does play 12...a5 it seems that Rc1 is not a particularly useful move. For example, 13.b3 Nd7 14.Bxg7 Kxg7 15.Qd4+ Kg8 16.Rfd1 as in Andersson-Christiansen, Hastings 1978/79, and now Black could have obtained an equal ending with 16...Qb6, but who wants to play an ending against Andersson? In Dokhoian-Glek, Bonn 1994, Black instead played 15...f6!? in order to control the dark squares. After 16.Rfd1 Nc5 17.Rb1 Qb8 18.Bf1 Rd8 19.Qe3 e5 20.Rd2 Ne6 21.Rbd1 b6 22.g3 Ra7 23.Bh3 Ng5 24.Bg2 Ne6, a draw was agreed. Black has equalised with the standard dark-squared strategy.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5
commentaryText: The correct move order. 12...Nd7?! was punished by 13.Bxg7 Kxg7 14.b4! in Smyslov-Golz, Polanica Zdroj 1968, when White has achieved a typical advantage.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4
commentaryText: The logical plan. It is now far more difficult for White to seize space on the queenside.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4 a4
commentaryText: This is a very interesting idea. Normally, this move would be met by b2-b4, ...a4xb3, a2xb3, with an opening of the queenside favourable to White. But here the rook has left a1, which means that Black gets counterplay along the a-file. The 'standard' 13...Nd7 is also playable, which after 14.Bxg7 Kxg7 leads to structures very similar to the main lines where White takes on g7. Normally White must play his pawn to f4 in two moves, but here White has played Qd3, where it is not well placed in this kind of structure. Timman-Wedberg, Amsterdam 1984, continued 15.Kh1 f6 16.Rcd1 Qe8 17.Qd4 Qf7 with equality.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4 a4 14.Kh1 Qa5
commentaryText: Black again delays ...Nd7, keeping White guessing, while making useful moves.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4 a4 14.Kh1 Qa5 15.Qe3
commentaryText: 15.Nd5 might be a better idea when Black has a choice of captures: a) White was successful in Dolmatov-Petursson, Reykjavik 1988, when after 15...Nxd5 16.exd5 Bxd4, Dolmatov played 17.dxc6!? 17...Bxb2 18.Rc2 Qb4 19.cxb7 and Black blundered with 19...Ra5?? 20.Rxb2 Qxb2 21.Rb1 with a lost position. It was probably better to play 18...a3 which seems okay for Black. It is noteworthy that White did not like the attractive 17.Qxd4 Bd7 18.Bd3 followed by f4-f5. b) Black had more success with 15...Bxd5 16.exd5 Nd7 in the game Petrakov-Mololkin, Moscow 1994, when after 17.Bxg7 Kxg7 18.Rfe1 Rfe8 19.Bf1 Nf6 20.Qd4 b6 21.h3 Qc5 22.Qd2 Ra7, Black had a solid position. White now mistakenly played the 'active' 23.b4 axb3 24.axb3, and Black took the a-file with 24...Rea8 and later won the game.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4 a4 14.Kh1 Qa5 15.Qe3 Nd7
commentaryText: Now, finally, Black plays the standard plan.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4 a4 14.Kh1 Qa5 15.Qe3 Nd7 16.Bxg7 Kxg7 17.Bg4 Qc5
commentaryText: Since this kind of ending is at least equal for Black due to White's bad bishop, Black wins time by threatening the exchange of queens.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4 a4 14.Kh1 Qa5 15.Qe3 Nd7 16.Bxg7 Kxg7 17.Bg4 Qc5 18.Qe2 Nf6 19.Bh3 e5
commentaryText: A very strong move which probably gives Black the advantage. He now threatens ...e5xf4 followed by ...Rae8, attacking the e4-pawn, which will be difficult to protect with the bishop offside on h3.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4 a4 14.Kh1 Qa5 15.Qe3 Nd7 16.Bxg7 Kxg7 17.Bg4 Qc5 18.Qe2 Nf6 19.Bh3 e5 20.f5 g5
commentaryText: Since the knight on f6 is a mighty defender, Black does not fear the possibility of a white kingside attack.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4 a4 14.Kh1 Qa5 15.Qe3 Nd7 16.Bxg7 Kxg7 17.Bg4 Qc5 18.Qe2 Nf6 19.Bh3 e5 20.f5 g5 21.Bg4 h6 22.h4 Rh8 23.Bh5 Kf8 24.Nd5 Bxd5 25.cxd5 Qa5 26.Rc4 b5 27.Rc3
commentaryText: This is a very interesting position. Place the white h-pawn on h2 and the bishop on d3, and White would be winning. Yet here the pawn on h4 secures Black counterplay on the kingside since White will never be able to close it comfortably. It is difficult to say who is better, but Black seems to have more than sufficient counterplay.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4 a4 14.Kh1 Qa5 15.Qe3 Nd7 16.Bxg7 Kxg7 17.Bg4 Qc5 18.Qe2 Nf6 19.Bh3 e5 20.f5 g5 21.Bg4 h6 22.h4 Rh8 23.Bh5 Kf8 24.Nd5 Bxd5 25.cxd5 Qa5 26.Rc4 b5 27.Rc3 Ke7 28.Rfc1 Ra7 29.Bf3 Rd7 30.a3 Rb8 31.Rc6 Qd8 32.Qe1 Qg8
commentaryText: Black defends c7, but White will break through eventually. The only question is: will Black be able to break through on the kingside? Black's last moves might seem passive, but now he is ready 33...gxh4 and 34...Qg5. White cannot find a way to meet this.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4 a4 14.Kh1 Qa5 15.Qe3 Nd7 16.Bxg7 Kxg7 17.Bg4 Qc5 18.Qe2 Nf6 19.Bh3 e5 20.f5 g5 21.Bg4 h6 22.h4 Rh8 23.Bh5 Kf8 24.Nd5 Bxd5 25.cxd5 Qa5 26.Rc4 b5 27.Rc3 Ke7 28.Rfc1 Ra7 29.Bf3 Rd7 30.a3 Rb8 31.Rc6 Qd8 32.Qe1 Qg8 33.Qb4 Rbd8 34.Be2 gxh4 35.R6c3 Qg5 36.Bxb5 Rg8 37.Bf1 Qf4 38.Rc7 Rgd8
commentaryText: Finally, it is Black who is making the threats. 38...h3 was winning, but in time trouble Black plays it safe. He will win in the end because his knight is so much stronger than the white bishop.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 Nf6 7.Nc3 0-0 8.Be2 d6 9.0-0 Bd7 10.Rc1 Nxd4 11.Bxd4 Bc6 12.Qd3 a5 13.f4 a4 14.Kh1 Qa5 15.Qe3 Nd7 16.Bxg7 Kxg7 17.Bg4 Qc5 18.Qe2 Nf6 19.Bh3 e5 20.f5 g5 21.Bg4 h6 22.h4 Rh8 23.Bh5 Kf8 24.Nd5 Bxd5 25.cxd5 Qa5 26.Rc4 b5 27.Rc3 Ke7 28.Rfc1 Ra7 29.Bf3 Rd7 30.a3 Rb8 31.Rc6 Qd8 32.Qe1 Qg8 33.Qb4 Rbd8 34.Be2 gxh4 35.R6c3 Qg5 36.Bxb5 Rg8 37.Bf1 Qf4 38.Rc7 Rgd8 39.Qe1 Nxe4 40.R7c4 Ng3+ 41.Kg1 Qxf5 42.Rxa4 Qg5 43.Rc2 f5 44.Bb5 Rb7 45.Ba6 Rb3 46.Qa5 Rxb2 47.Rc7+ Kf8 48.Rb4 Rd2 49.Rb1 h3
commentaryText: A hard-fought battle, where Black defended well. His knight on f6 kept things under control and then he went onto the offensive. White's ideas with Qd3 are not particularly dangerous but lead to complicated struggles with mutual chances.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 d6 7.Be2 Nh6
commentaryText: The immediate 6...Nh6 has, of course, also been tried, but generally, it just transposes. A few exceptions are mentioned in the next game. First recommended by Simagin. Of course, Tarrasch's maxims teach that it is bad to place the knight on the edge of the board, but here it does have some use. The only other square for the knight is f6, where it temporarily hinders Black by blocking the g7-bishop and the f-pawn.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 d6 7.Be2 Nh6 8.0-0 0-0 9.Qd2
commentaryText: At the time of the game, this move was considered good for White, but now it is not very highly regarded. The game transposes to the Classical System with 9...Re8 without Black having played ...Re8! In that variation Black plays 9...Re8, waiting to counter 10.Qd2 with 10...Ng4 but here Black get a better version since the rook is not urgently needed on e8 with this structure. The standard 9.Nc3 is considered (by transposition) in the next game.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 d6 7.Be2 Nh6 8.0-0 0-0 9.Qd2 Ng4 10.Bxg4 Bxg4 11.Nc3 Qa5
commentaryText: Nowadays, this is regarded as the main line. The alternatives are: a) 11...Rc8 has been played on occasion. A horrible example is Bhend-Keres, Zurich 1959, when Black had a terrible position after 12.b3 a6 13.Rac1 Qa5 14.h3 Bd7 15.Nxc6 bxc6? 16.c5 Be6 17.Nd5! although Keres later managed to draw. Better was 15...Bxc6 16.Nd5 Qd8, followed by ...b7-b5 with reasonable play. b) Langeweg-Velimirovic, Amsterdam 1974, saw 11...Bd7 12.f4 Rc8 13.b3 Qa5 14.Rac1 f5 15.exf5 gxf5 16.Nde2 Be6 17.Ng3 Rfd8 18.Rfd1 Bf7 19.Nb5! Qxd2 20.Rxd2 a6 21.Nc3 e6 22.Bb6 Rd7 23.Na4 and Black has too many weaknesses. Normally Black is not afraid of endgames in the Maroczy, but if he has played ...f7-f5, they are generally dangerous for Black.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 d6 7.Be2 Nh6 8.0-0 0-0 9.Qd2 Ng4 10.Bxg4 Bxg4 11.Nc3 Qa5 12.Rac1
commentaryText: Interestingly, Geller has no confidence in 12.f4!?, which had brought Petrosian a quick victory against Heinicke 12 years earlier. In that game, Black had played 12...Nxd4 13.Bxd4 e5 14.fxe5 dxe5 15.Be3 Rad8 16.Qf2 f5? 17.Bc5 Rf7 18.h3 and White picked up a piece. 12...Bd7 followed by ...Rc8 seems more logical, after which Black has reasonable play. A sign that 12.f4!? cannot be so bad for Black is the fact that Larsen was ready for it - and Geller did not dare play it!

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 d6 7.Be2 Nh6 8.0-0 0-0 9.Qd2 Ng4 10.Bxg4 Bxg4 11.Nc3 Qa5 12.Rac1 Rfc8 13.b3 a6 14.Rc2
commentaryText: Played to prevent ...b7-b5, but this move misses its objective. Better is 14.Nxc6!, which was introduced by a young Kasparov against Ivanov, Daugavpils 1978, which continued 14...Rxc6 15.Bh6! Rac8 (trading Black's best piece, since 15...Bh8 16.Nd5 Qd8 17.Qg5! is winning) 16.Bxg7 Kxg7 17.f4 f6 18.Kh1 b5 19.f5 g5 with complex play. Kasparov writes that 17.Qb2 is preferable, giving White an edge after 17...f6 18.Nd5, though surely it is not a lot. This idea was tried out in Popovic-Abramovic, Novi Sad 1985, and after 15.Bd4 Be6 16.Bxg7 Kxg7 17.Qb2 f6 18.Nd5 Qd8 19.a4 Rac8 20.Rcd1 Rc5, Black's set-up was solid and he can try for ...b7-b5.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 d6 7.Be2 Nh6 8.0-0 0-0 9.Qd2 Ng4 10.Bxg4 Bxg4 11.Nc3 Qa5 12.Rac1 Rfc8 13.b3 a6 14.Rc2 b5
commentaryText: Very strong. After 15.cxb5, Black has the pleasant choice between 15...axb5 16.Ndxb5 Nb4 17.Rb2 Bd7 with fine compensation, 15...Nxd4 16.Bxd4 Bxd4 17.Qxd4 axb5, and the spectacular 15...Bxd4!? 16.Bxd4 axb5, since 17.Be3 Nb4 is annoying for White. It may seem odd to give up the dark-squared bishop, but White must defend his queenside and will not get a mating attack.

source.title: The Sicilian Accelerated Dragon (20th Anniversary Edition)
source.author: Peter Heine Nielsen & Carsten Hansen

moveSequence: 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 g6 5.c4 Bg7 6.Be3 d6 7.Be2 Nh6 8.0-0 0-0 9.Qd2 Ng4 10.Bxg4 Bxg4 11.Nc3 Qa5 12.Rac1 Rfc8 13.b3 a6 14.Rc2 b5 15.Nd5 Qxd2 16.Rxd2 Bxd4 17.Bxd4 Rab8
commentaryText: Black keeps things under control. If now 18.c5 Be6! 19.cxd6 Bxd5 20.exd5 Nxd4 21.Rxd4 exd6, he gains a huge advantage due to his control of the c-file.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6
commentaryText: Question: Why did Black play this move rather than developing a knight with 2...Nc6? Answer: Perhaps because of the Rossolimo Variation with 3 Bb5. This is a line in which Black can struggle to get counterplay, especially if White captures on c6, doubling Black's pawns. This is also the reason I recommend that Black plays 2...g6 in this book.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 Bg7
commentaryText: This was popular at the time of the game, but is very risky for Black because of 4 dxc5 or 4 d5. 3...cxd4 is a better move. White can then play 4 Qxd4, developing quickly and attacking the rook on h8, which is certainly playable, but Black has 4...Nf6, intending to develop his other knight and gaining time on White's queen.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 Bg7 4 Nc3
commentaryText: Allowing Black to transpose back into a main line of the Accelerated Dragon.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 Bg7 4 Nc3 cxd4 5 Nxd4 Nc6 6 Be3 Nf6 7 f3
commentaryText: A mistake by White. 7 Bc4 is the standard move and best, with 7 Qd2 another move frequently seen at club level. After 7...0-0 (7...Ng4!? 8 Nxc6 dxc6! 9 Qxd8+ Kxd8 is also quite interesting, echoing Larsen's play against the Qxd4 lines in Games 67 and 68) 8 f3 we're back in our main game, while the immediate 8 0-0-0 is well met by 8...Ng4, depriving White of his important dark-squared bishop. Here 8 Nb3 has been very rare, but may well be best, and against which Black should just go 8...d6 followed by ...Be6, as per our approach in Chapter Seven.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 Bg7 4 Nc3 cxd4 5 Nxd4 Nc6 6 Be3 Nf6 7 f3 0-0 8 Qd2
commentaryText: Question: If 8...d5 is such a problem, why does White not prevent it with 8 Bc4? Answer: He can certainly do that, though Black then has 8...Qb6, directly threatening the b2-pawn and with veiled threats against the knight on d4. After 9 Bb3 there might follow 9...Nxe4 10 Nd5! Qa5+ 11 c3 Nc5 12 Nxc6 dxc6 13 Nxe7+ Kh8 14 Nxc8 Raxc8, with Black having the more comfortable game already.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 Bg7 4 Nc3 cxd4 5 Nxd4 Nc6 6 Be3 Nf6 7 f3 0-0 8 Qd2 d5 9 Nxc6 bxc6 10 exd5
commentaryText: 10 e5 Nd7 11 f4 Rb8 is very promising for Black.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 Bg7 4 Nc3 cxd4 5 Nxd4 Nc6 6 Be3 Nf6 7 f3 0-0 8 Qd2 d5 9 Nxc6 bxc6 10 exd5 Nxd5 11 Bd4
commentaryText: In his notes Velimirovic mentioned 11 0-0-0, but this looks very bad for White after 11...Bxc3 12 bxc3 Qa5, threatening 13...Qa3+.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 Bg7 4 Nc3 cxd4 5 Nxd4 Nc6 6 Be3 Nf6 7 f3 0-0 8 Qd2 d5 9 Nxc6 bxc6 10 exd5 Nxd5 11 Bd4 e5
commentaryText: Velimirovic was never reluctant to sacrifice material, and here he plays the sharpest move which leads to the sacrifice of the exchange. Question: Does Black have to play this way? Answer: No, there was a quieter route to an edge via 11...Bxd4 12 Qxd4 e5 13 Qd2 Nxc3 14 Qxc3 e4 15 Be2 exf3 16 Bxf3 Rb8 17 b3 (17 0-0 Qb6+ 18 Rf2 Qxb2 wins a pawn) 17...Re8+ 18 Kf2 Qb6+, with a strong initiative.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 Bg7 4 Nc3 cxd4 5 Nxd4 Nc6 6 Be3 Nf6 7 f3 0-0 8 Qd2 d5 9 Nxc6 bxc6 10 exd5 Nxd5 11 Bd4 e5 12 Bc5 Nxc3 13 Bxf8
commentaryText: 13 bxc3 Re8 is just better for Black because his kingside pawn majority is healthy, whereas White's doubled c-pawns will be unable to create a passed pawn.

commentaryText: After 14 Qxc3 there follows 14...e4! 15 Qxc6 (15 Qa5 exf3 16 0-0-0 Bg4 is also very good for Black) 15...Qb4+ 16 c3 Qxb2 17 Qe8+ Bf8, which is winning for Black according to the engines.

commentaryText: Question: What happens now after 19 Rb1? Answer: In that case Black wins with 19...Bc3! 20 Qxc3 Qe3+ 21 Kf1 Be2+ 22 Ke1 (or 22 Bxe2 Qxc3, etc) 22...Bxd3+ 23 Kd1 Be2+ 24 Ke1 Qxc3+, picking up White's queen and the game.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 Nc6 5 Nc3 Bg7 6 Be3 Nf6 7 Bc4 0-0 8 Bb3 Re8
commentaryText: As noted in the game above, it is also possible for White to act against an early ...d7-d5 by playing 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 Nc6 5 Nc3 Bg7 6 Be3 Nf6 and now 7 Bc4, but here too there are unpleasant surprises in store. A recent discovery has been the line 7...0-0 8 Bb3 Re8!?, as pioneered by Vadim Zvjaginsev. When White's attempts to treat this as a standard Dragon with 9 f3, he runs into either 9...e6, intending 10...d5, or even the immediate 9...d5. This line is no joke for White as he will once again find himself facing ferocious counterplay.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 g6 5 Nc3 Bg7 6 Be3 Nf6 7 Bc4 0-0
commentaryText: Threatening 8...Nxe4, and if 9 Nxe4 d5.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 g6 5 Nc3 Bg7 6 Be3 Nf6 7 Bc4 0-0 8 Bb3
commentaryText: A prudent retreat. We saw that 8 f3?! Qb6! is pretty effective for Black in our opening game, and 8 Qd2?! Ng4 is even worse for White.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 g6 5 Nc3 Bg7 6 Be3 Nf6 7 Bc4 0-0 8 Bb3 Re8
commentaryText: Question: What is the idea? Answer: There are several. Firstly, it prepares to meet 9 f3 with 9...e6 or even 9...d5. Secondly, the rook can be well placed on e8 because it defends e7 and can allow Black to sidestep White's attempts to exchange dark-squared bishops, via Qd2 and Bh6, with ...Bh8.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 g6 5 Nc3 Bg7 6 Be3 Nf6 7 Bc4 0-0 8 Bb3 Re8 9 h3
commentaryText: A known idea, preventing Black from playing ...Nf6-g4 at an annoying moment. Zvjaginsev played this in an earlier game in the same tournament against Vavulin. That one proceeded 9 Nxc6 dxc6 10 Qxd8 Rxd8 11 f3 b6 12 Kf2 Ba6 13 Rhd1 Nd7 14 h3 Kf8, with very comfortable equality for Black and an eventual draw.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 g6 5 Nc3 Bg7 6 Be3 Nf6 7 Bc4 0-0 8 Bb3 Re8 9 h3 d6 10 0-0 Na5
commentaryText: A strong move, looking to eliminate White's strong bishop.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 g6 5 Nc3 Bg7 6 Be3 Nf6 7 Bc4 0-0 8 Bb3 Re8 9 h3 d6 10 0-0 Na5 11 f4 b6 12 e5 Nxb3 13 exf6 Nxd4 14 fxe7
commentaryText: Question: What does Black do after 14 fxg7? Answer: He can move his knight with 14...Nf5 and then take the g7-pawn at his leisure.

commentaryText: Black has a weak pawn on d6 and there are vulnerable squares in front of it, but this is more than compensated for by the pressure on the a8-h1 diagonal. White would really like his f4-pawn back on f3 in order to counteract this.

commentaryText: Now White deteriorates rapidly. Best was 20 Nd5, after which 20...Rae8 (20...Bxb2 21 f5 is quite dangerous for Black) 21 f5 gxf5 22 c3 is still better for Black, but not decisively so.

commentaryText: This retreat does not help White's cause. 21 Rd3 was a better idea: for example, after 21...Ba6 22 Rdd1 Bxc3 23 bxc3 Bb7 White can start trying to exchange pieces with 24 Bd2.

commentaryText: Creating even more weaknesses, though White would not have relished the thought of the black pawn coming to h4.

commentaryText: 26...d4! wins immediately, but it would have to be calculated. After 27 Bxd4 there might follow 27...Bxd4+ 28 Rxd4 Rxd4 29 cxd4 Re2 30 Nf2 Qc2, leaving White helpless against the threat of...Qd2 followed by...Qe1+.

commentaryText: Another inaccuracy, perhaps suggesting that one or both players might have been short of time. 28...Qc4 would have been more accurate, one of the points being that 29 Bxf6 is met by 29...Rxf4.

commentaryText: Missing a good chance to confuse matters with 29 f5: for example, 29...gxf5 30 Qg3+ Kh7 31 Bxf6 Rxf6 32 Nf2 intends to bring the knight to h3 then g5.

commentaryText: After this White gets counter-chances. Recentralizing the queen with 30...Qc4 would have been better.

commentaryText: A wrong check. White should play 35 Nf2: for example, 35...Be8 36 Qg5 Rg6 37 Qxh5 keeps White very much in the game.

commentaryText: A final blunder, which is highly suggestive of time trouble. 38 Qd6 would have left the issue very much in doubt.

moveSequence: 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 Nc6 5 c4
commentaryText: At this point the reader may be wondering why the Accelerated Dragon is not more popular than it is, which is partly due to concern about the Maroczy Bind with 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 Nc6 5 c4. This has long been thought to be a critical test, with White obtaining an annoying space advantage. Yet here too it seems that Black can get excellent counterplay if he knows what he is doing in the critical Gurgenidze System, 5...Nf6 6 Nc3 d6. After either 7 f3 or 7 Be2 Black can take on d4 and draw the white queen into the open.

commentaryText: Transposing into an Accelerated Dragon via a 1 Nf3 move order. This illustrates the transpositional advantages of this line, which can be used as the basis of a defence against both 1 Nf3 and 1 c4.

commentaryText: Regarded as critical, forcing the exchange of queens and relying on White's extra space.

commentaryText: This has been seen as the critical test for Black, cracking down on his attempts to play the freeing ...f7-f5.

moveSequence: 1 Nf3 c5 2 c4 g6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 Nc6 5 e4 Nf6 6 Nc3 d6 7 Be2 Nxd4 8 Qxd4 Bg7 9 Be3 0-0 10 Qd2 Be6 11 f3 Qa5 12 Rc1 Rfc8 13 b3 a6 14 Na4 Qxd2+ 15 Kxd2 Nd7 16 g4 Rcb8
commentaryText: The key move, which changes the assessment of this line. Question: What is the idea? Answer: At the moment Black simply wants to play...b7-b5. Question: What had Black played previously? Answer: In earlier games attention was focussed on 16...f5, but Black was struggling after 17 exf5 gxf5 18 h3 Rf8 19 f4 Rad8 20 g5, despite the best efforts of expert practitioners. For example, 20...Bf7 was introduced by Gadir Guseinov, a noted Accelerated Dragon expert, but 21 Rhd1 (21 Bf3!?) 21...e5 22 Ke1 exf4 (22...Rfe8!? is a possible improvement) 23 Bxf4 Be5 24 Bxe5 Nxe5 25 Nc3 Be6 26 Kf2 was better for White in Bu Xiangzhi-G.Guseinov, Doha 2014. Although Black lost the featured game, it was certainly not because of the opening and the key move 16...Rcb8; in fact Black was better at certain stages of the game. From a theoretical point of view this move puts the ball firmly in White's court.

moveSequence: 1 Nf3 c5 2 c4 g6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 Nc6 5 e4 Nf6 6 Nc3 d6 7 Be2 Nxd4 8 Qxd4 Bg7 9 Be3 0-0 10 Qd2 Be6 11 f3 Qa5 12 Rc1 Rfc8 13 b3 a6 14 Na4 Qxd2+ 15 Kxd2 Nd7 16 g4 Rcb8 17 Nc3 b5 18 Nd5 Bxd5 19 cxd5 Nc5
commentaryText: The key move, blocking the c-file at the cost of a pawn.

moveSequence: 1 Nf3 c5 2 c4 g6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 Nc6 5 e4 Nf6 6 Nc3 d6 7 Be2 Nxd4 8 Qxd4 Bg7 9 Be3 0-0 10 Qd2 Be6 11 f3 Qa5 12 Rc1 Rfc8 13 b3 a6 14 Na4 Qxd2+ 15 Kxd2 Nd7 16 g4 Rcb8 17 Nc3 b5 18 Nd5 Bxd5 19 cxd5 Nc5 20 b4
commentaryText: White wants to penetrate with his c1-rook, but Black will get counterplay with...a6-a5. Black also gets play after the alternatives, for example: a) If White takes the pawn with 20 Bxc5 dxc5 21 Rxc5, Black gets a blockade on the dark squares with 21...Bh6+ 22 Kd3 Bf4, preventing White's pawns from moving and at the same time defending the c7-square. The engines still give White a plus at this point, but that is only because they value material in their assessment algorithms. b) 20 h4 Rc8 21 h5 e6 22 dxe6 Nxe6 23 h6 Be5 (23...Bb2! is even better) 24 Rxc8+ Rxc8 25 Rc1 Rxc1 26 Kxc1 Nd4 gave Black enough play to draw in G.Ilzig-J.De Mingo Matias, correspondence 2019.

commentaryText: 31...Rh2 seems to be Black's simplest move; he just wants to take the h-pawn. The game might then end in a draw by repetition after 32 Ra5 Rxa5 33 Rxa5 Rxh3 34 Ra7 Kf8 35 Ra8+ Kg7 36 Ra7 Kf8, etc.

commentaryText: In playing 'for a win', White puts himself in serious danger. He should have played 32 Rc2 when the game should be a draw.

commentaryText: 32...Rd2+! 33 Kc3 Ra1 would have put White in serious trouble because Black is going after the f3-pawn with one of his rooks.

commentaryText: Black might have been worried about 33...Rd2+ 34 Kc3 Rxd6 35 e5 Rh6 36 e6, but 36...f6 is solid enough here.

commentaryText: After this it should be equal, whereas 34...Rxf3+ 35 Ke2 Re3+ 36 Kf2 Rxh3 would have left Black with all the chances.

commentaryText: The lines where White plays Nxc6 are not generally considered dangerous for Black. The most important one occurs after 1 e4 c5 2 Nf3 g6 3 d4 cxd4 4 Nxd4 Nc6 5 Nc3 Bg7 6 Be3 Nf6 7 Nxc6 as after 7...bxc6 8 e5 Black's knight on f6 should go back to g8. Even so it seems that White cannot make much out of his lead in development.

commentaryText: The human move, but not the only one. The engines also like the immediate 12...Nf5, with humans having played this way too. For example, 13 Bf2 (13 dxe7 Qxe7 14 Bf2 Be6 15 g4 Rab8 gave Black a powerful attack in Hong Xing-Lu Miaoyi, Shenzhen 2023) 13...Nxd6 (13...Rb8 does not work because of 14 d7 Bxd7 15 Qxd7 Qa5 16 Qxa7 Qb4 17 Qa3 Qxa3 18 bxa3 Bxc3 19 Rd3, with White emerging with the better endgame) 14 Bd4 Bh6!? (14...Bxd4 15 Qxd4 Bg4 16 Rd2 Qb6 is simple and equal, but Black will find it difficult to win games like this) 15 Bd3 Bg4 16 Rde1 Rb8 17 a3 Qd7 18 h4?! Rfd8! 19 g3 c5 20 Bxc5 Nc4 won quickly for Black in E.Tairova-N.Chadaev, Moscow 2006.
